title: SMOTE and Mirrors: Exposing Privacy Leakage from Synthetic Minority Oversampling
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: A generator that interpolates between real points leaves geometric structure that lets an adversary both identify and recover the real records.
layout: 3 zones, left-to-right; data cylinders feed attacker characters with geometric insets
description: A hand-drawn, sketch-style diagram. On the left, a blue cylinder of real data (X_real^0 with n_0 records, plus an orange slab X_real^1 with n_1 records) is combined with SMOTE(X_real) through an arrow. The result is a taller cylinder with a purple slab of synthetic minority records (X_synth^1, n_0-n_1) added. In the middle and right, the augmented cylinder goes through an arrow to a red devil-faced attacker labelled DistinSMOTE, with a dotted SMOTE() bubble. A red 'distinguishes' arrow points to a small orange real-records cylinder. A synthetic-only purple cylinder goes to a second devil labelled ReconSMOTE, with a red 'reconstructs' arrow pointing back to the real records. Two small insets show orange real points at the ends of a dashed line, with purple synthetic points between them. One inset has a circled 'reconstructed' point. The eye goes first to the red devils and the bright cylinders.
caption: DistinSMOTE and ReconSMOTE attacks vs. augmented/synthetic data generated by SMOTE.
abstract: The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is one of the most widely used methods for addressing class imbalance and generating synthetic data. Despite its popularity, little attention has been paid to its privacy implications; yet, it is used in the wild in many privacy-sensitive applications. In this work, we conduct the first systematic study of privacy leakage in SMOTE: we begin by showing that prevailing evaluation practices, i.e., naive distinguishing and distance-to-closest-record metrics, completely fail to detect any leakage and that membership inference attacks (MIAs) can be instantiated with high accuracy. Then, by exploiting SMOTE's geometric properties, we build two novel attacks with very limited assumptions: DistinSMOTE, which perfectly distinguishes real from synthetic records in augmented datasets, and ReconSMOTE, which reconstructs real minority records from synthetic datasets with perfect precision and recall approaching one under realistic imbalance ratios. We also provide theoretical guarantees for both attacks. Experiments on eight standard imbalanced datasets confirm the practicality and effectiveness of these attacks. Overall, our work reveals that SMOTE is inherently non-private and disproportionately exposes minority records, highlighting the need to reconsider its use in privacy-sensitive applications and as a baseline for assessing the privacy of modern generative models.
